newsitem.title: USA: Human Mars mission beyond current technology.
newsitem.headline: Human Mars mission beyond current technology.

text.p: Humans are unlikely to follow in the tracks of the solar-powered buggy roving the surface of Mars unless there are major technology breakthroughs on Earth, scientists said on Tuesday.

The recent Pathfinder mission to Mars sparked new interest in sending astronauts to destinations beyond the Earth's orbit, but a National Research Council study dampens expectation of that happening soon.
"Today's technologies would not be able to sustain crews affordably on these types of missions," it said.

For example, sending a crew to Mars would take almost two years round-trip and it would be difficult and costly -- if not impossible -- to completely stock or replenish the necessary food, water and oxygen supplies.

"Although there are no immediate plans for sending a crew that far, NASA's long-term goals suggest that technologies for such planetary missions could be needed as soon as the year 2010," the NRC report said.
Funded by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the study evaluated the agency's research programmes for living and working in space and found them seriously lacking.

"NASA has not directed research and development to address, specific, long-term goals in human space exploration ... NASA staff and others working on human support projects often do not have clear objectives or know to whom they are responsible," it said.

The scientists said that even without plans for major human space exploration, NASA had "a basic mission" to develop new technologies and ought to be able to direct some of its resoureces in that direction.
They said the agency allocates less than $20 million a year to developing new human support systems for space travel.

"The situation has become so strained that many members of NASA management seem reluctant to admit that they are contemplating human exploration missions -- even missions that would be launched more than 20 years hence," they added.

The NRC recommended NASA focus on developing a self-contained, onboard life-support system to control the atmosphere, manage wastes and provide food and water as well as a reliable method for monitoring the air, water and food supplies for contaminants.

In addition, the agency needed to design new, lighter and more mobile spacesuits to allow astronauts to explore planet surfaces with different gravity forces. Today's spacesuits were designed for weightless environments.

Current technology can support human crews in space for missions in low orbit such as the U.S. shuttle and Russian Mir programmes, but they depend on ready resupply from Earth for oxygen, water and food.

The unmanned Pathfinder landed on the dusty surface of Mars July 4 after a seven-month journey of 309 million miles (497 million km). The mission marked the beginning of an ambitious U.S. programme over the next decade to explore Mars and determine if it ever supported life forms.
